notes.b: Every ecosystem sorts its organisms by how they get energy and nutrients. Producers bring energy in, consumers pass it along, and decomposers return the nutrients to the soil or water.
points: Producers are autotrophs: organisms that make their own food from simple inorganic substances, mostly by photosynthesis, using light energy. They include green plants, algae, phytoplankton (microscopic floating algae) and photosynthetic bacteria.

Producers are the entry point of energy and matter into every food chain, because no other group can turn light energy and inorganic substances into organic food. There is more on this in Photosynthesis as an anabolic process.

Consumers are heterotrophs, meaning they cannot make their own food and obtain energy and nutrients by eating other organisms. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers, e.g. rabbits, slugs, caterpillars and limpets.
Secondary consumers eat primary consumers, e.g. thrushes, frogs and crabs. Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers, e.g. sparrowhawks, foxes and herons.
A top (apex) consumer is at the end of a chain and is not normally eaten. Carnivores eat animals; omnivores eat plants and animals, e.g. badgers, foxes and humans.

Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, feed on dead organisms and waste. They secrete enzymes onto the dead matter and absorb the products (saprophytic nutrition), and so release minerals and CO₂ for producers to reuse.

Detritivores are animals that eat dead organic matter (detritus), e.g. earthworms and woodlice. They break it into smaller pieces, which gives decomposers a larger surface to act on, so decomposition is faster. There is more on this in Bacteria and fungi.
notes.tip: Be ready to define producer, consumer and decomposer, and to name the top consumers in a chain (tertiary consumers or top predators). Don't confuse detritivores (animals that eat dead matter) with decomposers (bacteria and fungi that secrete enzymes).

notes.b: A food chain shows who eats whom, and each step is a trophic (feeding) level. Following the chain shows how energy and nutrients are passed on from one organism to the next.
points: A trophic (feeding) level is the position an organism occupies in a food chain, according to how it obtains its energy. Producers are trophic level 1, primary consumers level 2, secondary consumers level 3 and tertiary consumers level 4.
A food chain is a sequence of organisms in which each is eaten by the next, showing the transfer of energy and nutrients from one trophic level to the next.
Arrows point from the organism that is eaten towards the organism that eats it, which is the direction of energy flow ("is eaten by").
Irish examples, one per ecosystem. Grassland: grass → rabbit → fox. Hedgerow or woodland: oak leaves → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk. Rocky shore: seaweed → periwinkle → crab → herring gull.
Two more Irish examples. Freshwater: phytoplankton → water flea → minnow → heron (or pike). Sea: phytoplankton → zooplankton → herring → seal.

Grazing food chains start with living producers. Detritus (decomposer) food chains start with dead organic matter, e.g. dead leaves → earthworm → blackbird. Much of the energy in a woodland passes through detritus chains.
Food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels, because so much energy is lost at each level that too little is left to support a further level.
notes.tip: Arrows point to the eater, in the direction of energy flow, not from predator to prey. Producers are trophic level 1, not 0, and decomposers are not given a trophic level number. If asked why chains are short, say that energy is lost at each level.

notes.b: Real organisms rarely eat just one thing or get eaten by just one thing. A food web joins the separate food chains of an ecosystem into one network, which is why it is a more realistic picture.
points: A food web is a set of interlinked food chains in an ecosystem. It is more realistic than a single chain because most organisms eat more than one type of food and are eaten by more than one predator.
An organism may also feed at more than one trophic level, as an omnivore does, or as a fox does when it eats rabbits and also beetles.

Example grassland and hedgerow web to draw: grass → rabbit, grass → slug and grass → caterpillar; grass seeds → wood mouse; slug → thrush and caterpillar → thrush; rabbit → fox; wood mouse → fox and wood mouse → barn owl; thrush → sparrowhawk.
Decomposers (bacteria, fungi and earthworms) feed on dead material from every level of this web, because every organism eventually dies or produces waste.

Food webs show interdependence: a change in one population affects many others, directly through feeding and indirectly through competition for the same food. For example, the fox and the barn owl both eat wood mice, so they compete.
Diagram: the food web drawn with arrows pointing towards the consumer, organisms placed in rows by trophic level, and decomposers shown at the side receiving arrows from all levels.
notes.tip: You may be asked to construct a food chain or web from given information and to assign trophic levels. Draw every arrow pointing towards the eater, and define a food web as interlinked food chains.

notes.h: Energy flow and loss at each trophic level
notes.b: Energy enters an ecosystem once, as sunlight, and then dwindles as it is passed along a food chain. Most of it is lost at every step, and this explains both the shape of food chains and how we should feed people.
points: Energy enters ecosystems as light. Producers capture only a small fraction of the light that reaches them, around 1–2%, and store it as chemical energy in organic molecules. The rest is reflected, passes through leaves, or is lost as heat.
On average only about 10% of the energy in one trophic level is passed on to, and stored in, the next. The figure varies, roughly from 5% to 20%, so about 90% is lost at each transfer.

Respiration releases energy for movement, growth, active transport and keeping warm, and this ends up as heat lost to the surroundings. Birds and mammals lose the most, because they keep a constant body temperature.

Roots, bark, wood, bones and fur are left uneaten. Undigested food is egested as faeces, e.g. cellulose eaten by herbivores, and some energy is lost in excretory products such as urea. The energy in uneaten parts, faeces and dead bodies passes to decomposers, not to the next level.
Energy flows in one direction through an ecosystem and is not recycled: it enters as light and leaves as heat, so an ecosystem needs a continuous input of energy from the Sun.

Worked example (illustrative, using the 10% figure, not measured data): grass in a field stores 10 000 kJ, the rabbits that eat it store about 1 000 kJ, and the foxes about 100 kJ. A fourth level would store about 10 kJ, too little to support a population.
So there are fewer top predators, they often need large territories, and they are especially vulnerable to habitat loss.

Consequence for food production: eating plants directly, a shorter chain, uses the energy captured by crops more efficiently than feeding crops to animals and then eating the animals. A given area of land can therefore feed more people on plant-based food.
notes.tip: Energy is lost as heat, not "used up" or destroyed, and energy is not recycled. Give the transfer figure as "about 10%", and when asked where energy is lost, list respiration (heat), uneaten parts, faeces and excretory products.

notes.h: Transfer of nutrients between trophic levels
notes.b: Matter, unlike energy, passes along a food chain in the form of the food organisms eat. Some is lost at each level, but the ecosystem as a whole does not lose it, because decomposers send it back to producers.
points: Nutrients (matter) pass between trophic levels when one organism eats another. The carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids of the food are digested, absorbed and built into the consumer's own body (assimilated).

The elements involved are carbon, hydrogen and oxygen (in all biomolecules), nitrogen (in proteins and nucleic acids), phosphorus (in DNA, ATP and phospholipids), and minerals such as calcium and iron.

The amount of matter passed on also decreases at each level. Much of the food eaten is respired (carbon leaves as CO₂, hydrogen as water), egested in faeces, or excreted (nitrogen as urea or ammonia). So biomass (the mass of living material) also decreases up a food chain.

Unlike energy, matter is not lost from the ecosystem. Decomposers break down dead bodies, faeces and urine, releasing CO₂ and minerals such as nitrate, phosphate and ammonium that producers absorb and reuse, so nutrients cycle.
Contrast: energy flows one way through the ecosystem and is lost as heat, whereas nutrients cycle and are reused again and again.

Persistent substances that are not broken down or excreted, such as the insecticide DDT and mercury, pass up the food chain with the food and build up in the bodies of organisms at each level. They reach the highest concentrations in top consumers, which is called biomagnification.
Biomagnification is how DDT thinned the eggshells of birds of prey, which sit at the top of food chains and so carry the highest doses.

Diagram: a flow diagram of one food chain, with energy arrows getting narrower at each level, heat-loss arrows from every level, and a separate loop of nutrient arrows from all levels to decomposers and back to producers.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to contrast energy flow and nutrient cycling in an ecosystem. Say both halves: energy flows through and is lost as heat, while nutrients cycle and are reused.

notes.h: Using food webs to predict the effects of change
notes.b: A food chain or web is a model: a simplified picture that lets you work out what happens when one population goes up or down. Following a set method keeps the prediction logical.
points: The method has five steps. 1. Find the organisms that eat the changed species (its predators).
2. Find what the changed species eats (its food).
3. Find its competitors, the species that share its food.
4. Predict the direction of each change, giving reasons.
5. Note other effects, e.g. on plants and habitat.

Worked prediction using the food web above, if a disease such as myxomatosis (a viral disease of rabbits) kills most of the rabbits: (a) grass is grazed less and grows taller, providing more food and cover for slugs, caterpillars and wood mice.

Continued: (b) foxes lose their main prey, so they eat more wood mice and the eggs and chicks of ground-nesting birds, and fox numbers may fall. (c) Wood mice decline from the extra fox predation, so barn owls, which compete with foxes for wood mice, have less food.
Real outcomes depend on how flexible each predator's diet is, because a predator that can switch to other food will be affected less.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to predict and explain the effect on a food web of removing or adding one species. Work through predators, food and competitors, and give a reason for every direction of change.

notes.h: Trophic cascades, added species and the limits of models
notes.b: Changes spread through a web both when a species is removed and when one is added. Because the model is simplified, its predictions have limits.
points: Removing a top predator can cause a trophic cascade, a chain of effects passing down the food web. In Ireland, with no wolves, deer numbers increase, they browse young trees, and the woodland cannot regenerate, which affects every species that depends on the woodland.

Adding a species also spreads through a web. An invasive filter-feeder such as the zebra mussel removes phytoplankton at the base of a lake food web, reducing food for zooplankton and for the fish that eat them. There is more on this in Biodiversity loss and conservation.
Food chains and webs simplify real feeding, because many links are left out and diets change with the season and with age.
They usually show no numbers or amounts of energy, which pyramids do, and decomposers are often left out. There is more on models in general in Models.
notes.tip: For the trophic cascade, describe the mechanism (no wolves, more deer, browsing, no woodland regeneration) rather than claiming it is proven with figures for Ireland.

keyTerms.definition: An autotroph that makes its own food from simple inorganic substances, mostly by photosynthesis, forming trophic level 1.
An organism that makes its own food from simple inorganic substances, such as a green plant.
An organism that obtains its energy and nutrients by eating other organisms.
A herbivore that eats producers, forming trophic level 2.
A consumer that eats primary consumers, forming trophic level 3.
A consumer that eats secondary consumers, forming trophic level 4.
An organism, mainly a bacterium or fungus, that breaks down dead organisms and waste by secreting enzymes and absorbing the products.
An animal that eats dead organic matter, breaking it into smaller pieces that decomposers act on faster.
The position an organism occupies in a food chain, according to how it obtains its energy.
A sequence of organisms in which each is eaten by the next, showing the transfer of energy and nutrients.
A set of interlinked food chains in an ecosystem.
The digestion, absorption and building of food into the consumer's own body.
The build-up of a persistent substance, such as DDT or mercury, in the bodies of organisms at each level of a food chain, reaching its highest concentration in top consumers.
A chain of effects passing down a food web after a top predator is removed or added.

questions.prompt: Explain the terms (i) trophic level and (ii) food web, and give an example of a food chain from a named Irish ecosystem with four trophic levels.
questions.model: (i) A trophic level is the position an organism occupies in a food chain, according to how it obtains its energy. Producers are trophic level 1, primary consumers level 2, secondary consumers level 3 and tertiary consumers level 4. (ii) A food web is a set of interlinked food chains in an ecosystem. It is more realistic than a food chain because most organisms eat more than one type of food and are eaten by more than one predator. Example from a named Irish ecosystem, a hedgerow or woodland: oak leaves (producer, trophic level 1) → caterpillar (primary consumer, level 2) → blue tit (secondary consumer, level 3) → sparrowhawk (tertiary consumer, level 4).

questions.prompt: Consider how nutrients are transferred from one trophic level to the next, taking into account the loss of energy at each trophic level.
questions.model: Nutrients pass from one trophic level to the next when one organism eats another. The carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids of the food are digested, absorbed and built into the consumer's body. Energy, however, is lost at each transfer. Only about 10% of the energy in one trophic level is passed on to the next, and about 90% is lost, mainly as heat released by respiration, which keeps the consumer alive and active, and birds and mammals lose most this way. Energy is also lost in parts that are not eaten, in faeces that are egested, and in excretory products such as urea. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five levels: for example, 10 000 kJ stored in grass becomes about 1 000 kJ in rabbits, about 100 kJ in foxes, and only about 10 kJ at a fourth level. Matter is treated differently: much of it is also lost from the food chain in respiration, faeces and excretion, but the uneaten parts, faeces and dead bodies pass to decomposers, which release CO₂ and minerals such as nitrate and phosphate that producers reuse. So energy flows one way and is lost as heat, whereas nutrients cycle.

questions.prompt: Sample food web for a grassland and hedgerow: grass is eaten by rabbit, slug and caterpillar; grass seeds are eaten by wood mouse; slug and caterpillar are eaten by thrush; rabbit is eaten by fox; wood mouse is eaten by fox and barn owl; thrush is eaten by sparrowhawk. Predict and explain the effects on this food web if most of the rabbits died of disease.
questions.model: If most rabbits die of disease such as myxomatosis, grass is grazed less and grows taller, giving more food and cover for slugs, caterpillars and wood mice. Foxes lose their main prey, so they eat more wood mice and the eggs and chicks of ground-nesting birds, and fox numbers may fall. With more foxes eating them, wood mice decline, so barn owls, which also eat wood mice and compete with foxes for them, have less food. Fewer barn owls and wood mice also affect the thrushes and sparrowhawk only indirectly, through changes in food supply. The actual outcome depends on how flexible the diet of each predator is, because a fox or barn owl can switch to other prey.
